findings.title: Shared levels use unauthenticated cleartext HTTP
findings.code_excerpt:
public final static String USERLEVELS_GETPHP = "http://www.apo-games.de/apoSn4ke/get_level.php";
	public final static String USERLEVELS_SAVEPHP = "http://www.apo-games.de/apoSn4ke/save_level.php";
findings.entry_point: Downloaded bytes enter through urlConn.getInputStream()/input.readLine() at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:179-182; a locally authored level enters save(String level) at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:113 and is encoded at line 132.
findings.sink: The fixed http URLs at ApoSnakeConstants.java:5-6 are passed to URL/openConnection and cleartext request/response streams at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:121-137 and 162-179.
findings.data_path: Download: ApoSnakePanel.init() automatically calls loadUserlevels() at ApoSnakePanel.java:58-60; its thread at lines 79-86 calls ApoSnakeUserlevels.loadUserlevels() at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:22-30, then ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.load() at lines 153-209. Upload: ApoSnakeEditor.uploadString() at ApoSnakeEditor.java:227-230 calls ApoSnakeUserlevels.addLevel() at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:84-90, then save() at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:113-143.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker controlling the level server, DNS/route, or the victim's Wi-Fi answers the startup HTTP request with altered 11-line level records; the client accepts them as shared levels. The same attacker can read, change, or drop the level= POST during upload. This gives control over downloaded game content and enables the parser and availability attacks described below.
findings.preconditions: The build must grant network access and the Android version/network-security policy must permit cleartext HTTP; ApoSnake.isOnline() must return true (ApoSnake.java:48-52). A network-position attacker or malicious endpoint is needed; upload interception additionally requires the user to upload a solved editor level.
findings.validation_plan: Run the app/emulator with an HTTP-intercepting proxy or map www.apo-games.de to a controlled HTTP server. Launch while connected and observe the POST to get_level.php, then create, solve, and upload a level and observe the readable level= body sent to save_level.php. Modify the download response and confirm the altered level reaches the user-level menu; packet capture showing plaintext requests and successful response substitution proves the issue.

findings.title: Malformed downloaded level strings crash the level decoder
findings.entry_point: Every line with index 0 modulo 11 from the HTTP response is stored verbatim as a level at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:182-185.
findings.sink: ApoSnakePuzzleGame.loadLevel() derives array dimensions without checking length or range at lines 159-161, then indexes every declared cell with l.charAt(...) at line 167 and again at line 195.
findings.data_path: ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.load() stores the response at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:179-205; ApoSnakeUserlevels.getAllLevelsSorted() copies it at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:44-56 and assigns ApoSnakeLevel.editorLevels at line 30. The userlevels button invokes setPuzzleGame(-1, "", true) at ApoSnakeMenu.java:75-76; ApoSnakePanel.setPuzzleGame() calls loadLevel() at ApoSnakePanel.java:136-146, which selects editorLevels[p[0]] at ApoSnakePuzzleGame.java:138-155 and reaches the unchecked decoder.
findings.attack_scenario: A malicious server or HTTP man-in-the-middle returns one otherwise valid 11-line record whose level line is aa. Loading succeeds and exposes the userlevels button. When the victim taps it, width and height become 1, but l.charAt(2) at ApoSnakePuzzleGame.java:167 reads past the two-character string. The exception escapes every supplied caller and yields a repeatable game crash. A header byte such as _ produces a negative array dimension at line 161.
findings.preconditions: The network path in ApoSnake-01 must operate, the attacker must supply valid numeric values for the other ten record lines so sorting completes, and the victim must open userlevels. Direct poisoning by an ordinary UGC author is not established because save_level.php is not in the supplied source.
findings.validation_plan: Intercept get_level.php and serve these 11 lines in order: aa, 1.0, 1, 1, attacker, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1.0. Launch, wait for userlevels to appear, and tap it. An IndexOutOfBoundsException/StringIndexOutOfBoundsException with ApoSnakePuzzleGame.java:167 in the stack, or process termination at that action, confirms reachability.

findings.title: Unbounded shared-level response can exhaust memory and CPU
findings.entry_point: The server-controlled HTTP body enters DataInputStream at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:179 and is consumed until EOF at lines 182-207.
findings.sink: There is no response, line-length, or record-count bound before readLine() and the eleven ArrayList.add/valueOf branches at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:182-205; after reading, sortByUpload() performs nested insertion scanning at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:61-75.
findings.data_path: ApoSnakePanel.init() starts the download without a user gesture at ApoSnakePanel.java:58-60 and 79-86. ApoSnakeUserlevels.loadUserlevels() calls load() and then sortByUpload() at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:22-30, so attacker-controlled response size directly controls retained strings, boxed numbers, and the quadratic sort workload.
findings.attack_scenario: A malicious endpoint or HTTP man-in-the-middle streams a very long first line or hundreds of thousands of syntactically valid 11-line records. readLine() and the lists keep allocating until heap exhaustion; if EOF is sent first, equal timestamps make the nested insertion sort scan all prior entries and consume quadratic CPU. Because loading starts during initialization, the attacker can freeze or kill the game on launch without a menu selection.
findings.preconditions: The network and cleartext preconditions from ApoSnake-01 must hold and the attacker must control or replace the get_level.php response. A sufficiently large body relative to the Android heap is required.
findings.validation_plan: Use a controlled get_level.php response that repeatedly emits the valid 11-line record aa0, 1.0, 1, 1, attacker, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1.0, preferably on an emulator with a constrained heap. Repeat until the body contains enough records to exceed the heap, then launch the app. OutOfMemoryError or process death during lines 182-205 proves the memory path; a smaller completed body with equal timestamps and a profiler showing rapidly superlinear time in ApoSnakeUserlevels.sortByUpload() proves the CPU path.

findings.title: Editable local solved counter unlocks all built-in levels
findings.entry_point: The local solved integer comes from the app-private ApoSnakePref SharedPreferences opened at ApoSnake.java:43 and read directly at ApoSnakePanel.java:67-69.
findings.sink: The solved value is the only access decision in the touch loop at ApoSnakePuzzleChooser.java:84-87, which calls setPuzzleGame() for any index at or below it.
findings.data_path: ApoSnake.onCreate() obtains ApoSnakePref at ApoSnake.java:43; ApoSnakePanel.init() calls loadPreferences() at ApoSnakePanel.java:64; loadPreferences() reads solved and calls solvedLevel() at lines 67-69 and 179-181; ApoSnakePuzzleChooser.setSolved() accepts a larger value and only clamps it to MAX_LEVELS-1 at ApoSnakePuzzleChooser.java:66-77; touchedPressed() then uses it at lines 82-87.
findings.attack_scenario: A local user with root, app-UID instrumentation, or equivalent access stops the app and changes solved in ApoSnakePref to 999. On restart, setSolved() clamps it to the final level rather than rejecting it, and the chooser permits every built-in level. The gain is local progression cheating only, not code execution or a server-side privilege.
findings.preconditions: The attacker needs access beyond an ordinary unprivileged Android app because getSharedPreferences(..., 0) at ApoSnake.java:43 is app-private. Rooted-emulator or rooted-device access, or instrumentation under the app UID, is sufficient.
findings.validation_plan: On a rooted test emulator, force-stop the app, locate its ApoSnakePref.xml under the app data directory, and set the solved integer to 999, or use app-UID instrumentation to write the same preference. Relaunch and open the puzzle chooser. Being able to select the final built-in level, while a clean profile permits only the initial level, confirms the trust path.

notes: All 21 files actually present under the supplied source root were opened: 19 handwritten source files and two generated Java files. The snapshot places them below Users/eliahilse/Documents/GitHub/B/apogames/Android/ApoSnake/, which is why paths retain that root-relative prefix. It contains no AndroidManifest.xml, build script, resource files, PHP endpoint source, or gliblybits engine source; therefore network permission, cleartext policy, and server-side validation cannot be verified from this variant. The client sends only level= plus the encoded level at ApoSnakeUserlevelsLoad.java:132-133, but absent save_level.php source I did not claim that arbitrary direct submissions are accepted. BuildConfig.java:5 has DEBUG=true, but that alone does not prove manifest debuggability. Downloaded levels are passed to BitsLog at ApoSnakeUserlevels.java:53, but startup requests BitsLog.TYPE_NONE at ApoSnake.java:23 and the logger implementation is absent, so this was not reported as reachable information disclosure. ApoSnakeSolve.canBeSolved() exists at ApoSnakeSolve.java:21 but has no caller anywhere in the supplied tree, so its recursive search was treated as unreachable rather than another resource-exhaustion finding.
